In eastern Australia, Striped marsh frogs (Limnodynastes peronii) begin their life cycle as small, jelly-coated eggs deposited in foam nests at the water's surface. Upon eclosion, the emerging aquatic larva is initially endotrophic, relying on residual yolk stores before commencing filter feeding on suspended organic particles. The wet weight at birth, based on an average egg diameter of 1.5 millimeters, is approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a remarkably small mass that underscores the lecithotrophic strategy during the earliest developmental phase. Following yolk absorption completion, the actively growing tadpole enters a period of sustained feeding and somatic growth. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the time from hatching to the onset of metamorphosis has been documented as 84 days since birth . This developmental period, spanning roughly twelve weeks, allows sufficient time for the free-swimming larva to achieve the critical body size necessary for the profound morphological transformation associated with metamorphic climax, including limb bud development and gradual tail resorption.

Comparative morphometric data from field-collected specimens reveal clear sexual dimorphism in adult body size within this species. Females attain a significantly larger ultimate snout-vent length of 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], whereas males reach a maximum SVL of 7 centimeters [Li = 7 centimeters]. This divergence in body length is a common pattern among Australian myobatrachid frogs and is generally attributed to fecundity selection, as larger females can accommodate greater numbers of oviducal eggs. Corresponding to these length differences, the ultimate wet weight for adult females is estimated at 35.2 grams [Wwi = 35.2 grams], while adult males achieve a more modest maximum mass of 28.6 grams [Wwi = 28.6 grams]. These mass values, derived from length-weight scaling relationships established for similar-sized hylid frogs, provide a reliable proxy for the energetic investment each sex makes toward growth versus reproduction over the course of their lives.

Sexual maturation in Limnodynastes peronii occurs at a body size notably smaller than the ultimate adult dimensions. Onset of puberty in females is observed when individuals reach a snout-vent length of approximately 4.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.3 centimeters], a threshold representing about sixty percent of the maximum female length. This size at maturity suggests that females begin allocating resources to gametogenesis well before somatic growth has ceased, a life-history strategy common among frogs that experience moderate adult mortality rates. At the time of metamorphosis, when the recently metamorphosed juvenile first emerges onto land, the typical wet weight of a froglet is recorded at 0.4 grams . This substantial increase from the minute birth mass reflects the efficiency of filter-feeding and algal grazing during the aquatic tadpole stage, which allows the Gosner-stage larva to multiply its body mass by a factor of over two hundred prior to metamorphic climax.

Reproductive output in the Striped marsh frog is tied to seasonal environmental conditions and female body size. During the breeding season, gravid females deposit between 704 and 1400 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 704 and 1400 eggs per clutch], a fecundity range that correlates positively with maternal SVL. Under controlled thermal regimes of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], reproductive activity is typically limited to a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], resulting in a modest annual reproductive rate. This low frequency of breeding events is characteristic of many temperate-zone Australian ranids and likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by oogenesis in a seasonal environment where prey availability and suitable oviposition sites are temporally restricted. The foam nest, produced during amplexus and gametic union, provides a protective microhabitat for the developing embryos, buffering them against desiccation and thermal extremes while the yolk-laden eggs undergo cleavage and gastrulation.

Longevity data for this species indicate a relatively short life expectancy compared to larger-bodied anurans. The maximum recorded lifespan in wild populations has been estimated at approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days] when assessed at an average environmental temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This duration places Limnodynastes peronii among the shorter-lived members of its genus, likely a consequence of predation pressure from aquatic birds, snakes, and large invertebrates throughout the post-metamorphic stage. Natural mortality from senescence or age-related physiological decline typically follows the reproductive years, with most individuals completing their life cycle within the span of a few breeding seasons. The combination of early sexual maturation, high fecundity per clutch, and a relatively compressed adult lifespan suggests a life-history strategy adapted to fluctuating wetland environments where adult survival is uncertain but recruitment opportunities in favorable years can be substantial.
